Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette: Mateo was a fifty-four-year-old American of Latin American descent when he finally sat across from the clinician, but the weight he carried began years earlier in a fractured valley where he had traveled as a relief worker. He remembered the exact morning the sky turned gray with dust and sudden, sharp cracks tore through the quiet. He had been coordinating a distribution line, counting crates of medicine and grain, when the first shots rang out. In that moment, the familiar rhythm of helping strangers dissolved into a blur of running men and overturned trucks. He rarely spoke of the valley, but when the memory surfaced, his voice would tighten and his posture would freeze, his eyes fixing on the middle distance as he repeated the same fragmented details to anyone who asked. It followed him back to the states, settling into his bones. Now, when a car backfired on the interstate or fireworks popped over a neighborhood block, his shoulders seized before his mind could catch up. He didn’t just hear a noise; he felt the old panic rush back, a cold certainty that the ground was about to give way again. Over the months that followed, Mateo found himself flinching at ordinary closeness. At a client lunch for his logistics company, he had stiffened when a supplier reached across the table to tap his shoulder in congratulations. The contact sent a jolt through him, as if his skin had become a boundary meant to keep something out. He began avoiding crowded warehouses and stepping back during handshakes, telling himself it was just a preference for personal space, though what frightened him most was the sudden tightness in his chest whenever someone breached his personal circle. Positive moments proved just as disorienting. When his wife, Elena, laughed over Sunday brunch or when a deal at his firm closed with champagne toasts, Mateo felt a strange, unsettling confusion. He couldn’t quite let himself lean into the warmth. Joy felt like a language he had forgotten how to speak, and he often found himself excusing himself early, certain that if he stayed too long in the lightness, it would collapse. Mateo built routines to navigate the day. He began carrying a loaded pistol in a shoulder holster under his work jackets, the familiar weight against his ribs becoming a quiet anchor. He checked the safety during morning coffee and slept with it tucked under the mattress. At work, he kept his mind occupied by replaying the same questions over and over: why had the crossfire broken out that day, why had he been there, what was it about his presence that seemed to draw the violence. The questions looped through his head during inventory audits and late-night ledger entries, a quiet, relentless interrogation he couldn’t switch off. When the days grew long, he found himself manufacturing friction at home. He would pick arguments with Elena over misplaced keys or the way she loaded the dishwasher, letting the sharp exchange fill the room until the quiet settled. The pattern had become obvious to him, a habit that formed over weeks as the calendar turned. By the time he walked into the clinic, Mateo’s business was running on habit and exhaustion. The logistics office had become a place where he monitored every door, counted exits, and avoided the break room where staff gathered too closely. He had stopped going to company dinners, telling himself he was swamped with paperwork, though the truth was simpler: he was tired of feeling like a stranger in his own life. What finally brought him here was the evening Elena had tried to hug him and he had stepped back so quickly he’d knocked over a lamp. He had sat on the couch in the dark afterward, staring at his hands, wondering how he had lost the ability to just be present in his own marriage. He wasn’t sure he could ever return to the man he was before the valley, but he was desperate to stop running from the quiet, to learn how to sit through a laugh without bracing for the next crack of gunfire. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him figure out how to finally come home to himself.
